approachQuestion.prompt:
Repair queue

All n repairs are available at time zero. A single technician performs every repair without interruption, handling one at a time and leaving no idle gaps. Repair i takes positive duration p[i]. A repair’s completion time is the elapsed time when it finishes. Return the minimum possible sum of all completion times.

Example 1: p=[4,1,2] → 11: durations 1,2,4 finish at times 1,3,7.
Example 2: p=[3,3] → 9.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000; 1 ≤ p[i] ≤ 10^9; input is unsorted. Durations are arbitrary comparison keys rather than a small fixed universe. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Copy durations, sort ascending, then scan with elapsed=0 and total=0. Add each duration to elapsed and add elapsed to total.
options.feedback: For adjacent durations a>b, putting b first reduces the sum of their completion times by a-b; later completions are unchanged. Repeated exchanges remove inversions, so shortest-duration order minimizes the sum. Ties can appear in either order.

options.text: Use the original repair order, accumulating elapsed and total.
options.feedback: Input order has no optimality guarantee. For [3,1], it gives completion sum 7; ordering 1,3 gives 5.

options.text: Sort durations descending to finish the largest repair first.
options.feedback: This delays every shorter repair. For [3,1], descending order costs 7 instead of 5.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. The fixed frontier method copies the records, uses stable top-down comparison merge sort with one reusable linear merge buffer, and then makes the scan described above. Count copying, the buffer, and the recursion stack. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)
